In January 1991 the Winnipeg Harvest Food Bank received 306 calls for family food assistance. Last August the food bank got 1,335 calls. According to yesterday's report from the National Council on Welfare, our welfare recipients from almost all provinces are sinking further into poverty, unable to keep up with the rate of inflation.
In the west, except British Columbia, single parents have been hardest hit. The city of Winnipeg has already spent $58 million on welfare this year but needs another $12 million before the end of December. The Christmas Cheer Board will deliver 19,000 food hampers to needy families, a record number.
David Northcott, Director of Winnipeg Harvest, said that if he were standing here in the House of Commons he would say one thing to the government: "Feed us today".
The responsibility falls to the federal government. I urge the Prime Minister to remove the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan and help the poorest of the poor. Give them a good Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, November is CPR awareness month.
The Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada wants Canadians to know that the more people who learn CPR, the more potential there is for saving lives.
Every year some 45,000 Canadians die from heart attack. Last year more than 560,000 Canadians received training in basic life support, a 30 per cent increase over 1989.
While this increased interest in CPR is heartening, the number of newly trained people represents only 2 per cent of the Canadian population. That is weak ammunition to fight Canada's number one killer, heart disease and stroke.
The chances of surviving a heart attack improves the sooner medical pension is received. More than 80 per cent of heart attack victims who enter hospital without delay return home. Let us do what we can to ensure that more Canadians who suffer a heart attack do indeed return home.
Take CPR training.

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations Security Council's unanimous resolution 716 expresses unequivocally the collective will of the international community to bring an end to the deadlock and to achieve progress on the reunification of Cyprus.
The resolution reaffirmed that the solution must be based on one state of Cyprus comprising two politically equal communities. The Cyprus government stated that it is ready to abide by the terms of the resolution and called upon Turkey to do the same.
I believe the time has come for both sides to show some prudence and unanimity and make decisive efforts to find a solution to everyone's benefit.
The time of artificial and forceful division of people such as has happened in Cyprus belongs to the past. Such divisions only serve to deprive people of their basic human rights and freedoms and is totally out of step and intolerable in our changing world.
It is hoped that when the newly elected Government of Turkey takes over under the new Prime Minister Suleiman Demirel, it will be the beginning of a new era of co-operation and trust for a unified Cyprus.

across the country today. My province of Ontario and the riding of Northumberland are not immune to the blight.

For example, the proposed Canada clause suggests that sustainable development is a national issue, yet such areas as forestry and mining are identified as provincial jurisdictions.
In reality, however, as we all know the over-all environmental implications cannot be neatly isolated. There will always be a critical need for federal-provincial structures to ensure Canada's environmental integrity-

In a world which spent over $900 billion last year on arms, in which 40,000 children die each day from hunger and disease, in which the global environment is being devastated and in which there is a massive net outflow of capital from south to north, action is desperately needed. Le Canada doit faire beaucoup plus.
The UN has called on Canada to direct far more resources to serving basic human needs like clean water, primary education, primary health care and family planning.

Mr. Speaker, according to a recent study by the Toronto-Dominion Bank,
lay-offs, plant closures and cross-border shopping are all symptomatic of the diminishing ability of Canadian manufacturers to be competitive. The bank went on to say that one of the factors that helped weaken Canada's competitive position was the fluctuating level of the dollar in this country. Although the drop in value of the Canadian dollar in the early eighties helped manufacturers to remain competitive at the time, it did not help them in the long run, because manufacturers failed to realize that wage levels in Canada had increased, compared with those in the United States.
Considering proportionately higher wage increases, the rising value of the Canadian dollar and low growth productivity, it should come as no surprise that Canada's competitive position has weakened since 1985.

The policy of the government is a floating exchange rate. The exchange rate is established in the marketplace. The key to sustained economic recovery is to bring down interest rates. The way to bring down interest rates is to bring down inflation and inflationary pressures.
I remind the hon. member that interest rates have come down by 625 basis points since the high of May 1990. The hon. member will understand that the interest rate spreads have narrowed from 5.65 per cent to about 2.3 per cent or 2.4 per cent.
The goals and objectives that were established in the budget of February 1991, the key to economy recovery, the fundamentals are in place and we are meeting those targets. I can assure the hon. member that is the recipe for sustained growth and price stability.

Would the minister be prepared today to finally abandon
his high interest rate policy and give Canadian companies a chance to survive?

The hon. member is blaming all the economic ills on the value of the dollar. I point out to the hon. member that in 1976 when the Canadian dollar was worth $1.01 U.S., the British Columbia forest industry had a return on sales of 4.6 per cent and a return on assets of 5.1 per cent.
Back in 1985, when the dollar was worth 73 cents, they had a zero rate of return on sales and a zero rate of return on assets. So it does not necessarily follow that having a lower dollar will provide the cure for all the economic ills.
I will repeat this to the hon. member. The value of the dollar, the exchange rate on the dollar is established in the marketplace. The Bank of Canada intervenes to moderate the flow so that there are no inclines or declines that disrupt the marketplace. That is the role of the Bank of Canada and that is the policy that the Government of Canada is following.

I ask the Minister of Finance to acknowledge that his government anticipated that it would cause higher unemployment and poverty and quite simply planned ahead to make someone else pay the bill.

ment of Germany, and the Government of Britain all condemned those actions. Canada was silent.

the UI account; second, we must take into consideration the over-all fiscal objectives of the government, and third, we have to take into account the impact on the employees and the employers.

A great historian, a great American historian, Will Durand who was a Canadian by birth, had once said that history for the most part was guessing and that the rest was prejudice.

We celebrate today the 150th anniversary of the birth of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Born in Saint-Lin, north of

November 20,1991
Routine Proceedings
Montreal, he studied his humanities at the College de l'Assomption, then studied law at McGill University in Montreal.
First elected in 1871 to the Legislative Assembly of Quebec, he was elected to the House of Commons in 1874. In 1887, Laurier became the leader of the Liberal Party of Canada and, in the 1891 elections, he fought against Sir John A. Macdonald. But it was in 1896 that he became the first French-Canadian to be elected Prime Minister of Canada.

As Prime Minister, Laurier pushed for greater autonomy from Britain at a time when British imperialism was particularly popular in English Canada. The Manitoba school question and the Boer War were very contentious issues between English and French Canada, but Lauri-er's government eased the tension through statesmanship and firm leadership.
Perhaps his greatest achievements lay in the western parts of this great country. His government opened the door to thousands of immigrants who settled as farmers in the prairies. Thousands of others helped build two transcontinental railroads and it is under Laurier that ethnic neighbourhoods began to flourish in such cities as Winnipeg, Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal.
Then in 1905 under his premiership two Canadian provinces were created: Saskatchewan and Alberta. It was a great day in Canada's history.

His talents, especially as an orator, are legendary. He captivated the imagination of people from all walks of life. He inspired confidence to Canadians by showing them that their country had its place in the community of liberated and independent countries and that they should be proud of it. He opened Canada's doors to all the peoples of the world who found here peace, freedom and unprecedented prosperity.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Tilesday, November 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. McDermid that Bill C-38, an act to provide for the continuance of Telesat Canada under the Canada Business Corporations Act and for the disposal of the shares therein of Her Majesty in right of Canada, be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee E.

subtopic: TELESAT CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in this debate. I will begin by saying that this bill is definitely a bill whose time has not yet come.
Contrary to the argument of the government Telesat Canada clearly still serves an important public policy purpose. In particular it provides necessary satellite telecommunications services to the north and other remote regions of Canada.
Normally when I speak on bills I talk about the ramifications for my own region, the Atlantic, and in particular for my own province, Nova Scotia. This particular bill does not have specific ramifications in my province. It does however have ramifications in some of the remoter areas of the Atlantic, such as Labrador and parts of Newfoundland.
It seems particularly ironic to me that we would be looking at shortening the public policy life, indeed terminating the public policy life, of Telesat Canada, which provides such a necessary service to the remote areas of the country, at a time when we are all so concerned with pulling the country together rather than pushing it apart.
Government Orders
The government argues that the sale of Telesat will contribute to a healthy market driven telecommunications sector vital to the continued growth and diversity of the Canadian economy. One cannot argue that a healthy market driven telecommunications sector is not vital to the continued growth and diversity of the Canadian economy. Of course I would not even start to do so at any time. That is the kind of thing that we all believe in. Surely among the other things we all believe in is some sort of equivalency, if not total equality, of access to national matters of importance for all Canadians. What is of more importance in this information age than access to the information spread across the remote areas of this country by Telesat Canada?
The whole concept of a public policy role finds its greatest spiritual home in this country of ours because we are both blessed and cursed by our geography and population. The fact of our small population spread out across our gargantuan geography has been mentioned heaven only knows how many times in this Chamber. Every single one of our provinces has its remote areas. Our northern territories are remoteness personified vis-a-vis the centres of the country, whether the nation's capital or the larger cities. It is absolutely incredible to think that this government can actually give credence to the idea that Telesat Canada has ended its feasibility as a public policy organization.
According to the government the servicing of the northern and remote areas will not be affected by this new legislation. Who has the crystal ball over there? Who has suddenly become the soothsayer on the government side? With with the greatest respect to my colleagues on the government side, if they claim to have some sort of soothsayer who knows what will or will not happen as a result of the privatization of Telesat Canada I can only say that in the minds and hearts of Canadians, whether on this side of the House or across this country, there is not a whole lot of faith in the government's soothsaying abilities. We certainly have seen that it was not absolutely on target, considering the alleged benefits that it told us were going to come from the free trade agreement. We certainly have seen that all the good things that were supposed to stem from the GST are obviously not coming home to the minds and hearts of Canadians. Any soothsaying in that direction was clearly off the beaten track.

November 20, 1991
Government Orders
There are other areas of soothsaying where the government has fallen down. It was here, in this very Chamber, barely two weeks ago when the Minister of Finance told us the recession was over. The next day he had to eat his words. Indeed he has eaten his words, which is more than some Canadians will be able to do because of the inability to predict even the close future by this government.
When the government said to the people in the northern and remote areas of this country: "Do not worry, be happy, privatizing Telesat Canada is not going to affect your access to telecommunication services", I am afraid we have to say: "Gosh, we just do not believe you". "We do not even guarantee" said the hon. minister. I guess that makes me feel better. A guarantee from this government will make everyone in Canada sleep easier on that one. The touching faith of the hon. Minister of State for Finance and Privatization again overwhelms me-or should I say underwhelms me.
The government has also promised that Telesat will maintain its monopoly on the provision of satellite telecommunication services for the next 10 years. This provision, however, surely an oversight, has not been included in the legislation. Perhaps that alone should give rise to a certain amount of scepticism on the part of the Canadian people. It sounds unbelievable to think that the Canadian people would even be sceptical about this government. I can see the look of horror on the face of my colleague from Ottawa Centre but yes, the people of Canada are sceptical about promises that are written on water, not written in the legislation that the government is bringing forward.
Let me remind you that Telesat is the only Canadian carrier which provides commercial satellite facilities and services across the country.
I have some questions for the government. How will the government force the hand of a private sector company to provide services which may not be profitable, such as providing services to the northern and remote regions? We understand that there are good corporate citizens in this country. We all understand that. Everyone on this side of the House believes strongly, indeed fiercely, in a healthy business sector.
We stand here in recessionary times. We stand here when businesses are going bust all over this country. We stand here when bankruptcies are skyrocketing. Is a privatized company such as this one going to do the unprofitable in the face of the major profits they can make in the other areas of the country? The minister is again astounded that I should even voice such questions. I am just supposed to sit here and take it on trust. Well I am sorry. My constituents did not send me to Ottawa to take the government on trust. Take it on, yes, but not on trust.
The private sector does not have this responsibility. The responsibility lies squarely within the purview of the federal government. A federally owned corporation, put up to advance, promote and defend the cultural underpinnings of Canadian society, which is the mandate of this government, must remain the mandate of this government and must not be thrown away.
When business decides that certain things are unprofitable, they decide it according to their annual reports, their statements, their financial forecast, et cetera and rightly so. That is the way business works. Something this government does not quite understand is that governments and business are not absolutely identical. Government has responsibilities, particularly in the area of what the soul of a country is. If you sell off all of the tools that give you some ability to ensure that the soul of your country remains healthy, then is it any wonder we are in the troubled times we are in with regard to the whole state of this country? Is it any wonder?
I do not accuse the government of malfeasance. I accuse it of just not seeing; of perhaps not looking in the right direction; of perhaps not understanding what is necessary to keep this country on an even keel and on the straight track.
It is also the right of Canadians who live in northern and remote areas to have this access. The minister is nodding at me. I know he agrees. I know that. What I am asking him and his government is: What is your guarantee? You tell me you have a guarantee, but I hear you will, you will, you will. I should take it on trust. I cannot take it on trust. At the very least, why do you not amend the legislation and add in the provision of satellite telecommunications services for the next 10 years? That would be a small thing. It might make us all feel better.

Government intervention in the cultural sphere is crucial to providing Canadians with a common experience. Over the last several weeks we have listened to some of the problems we have with our common experience in this country. We are going through what I certainly hope will be the worst period in our history with regard to national unity and our sense of faith in the future. I hope nearly all members in this House will agree with me, that what we have been going through is the nadir, and it is not going to get any worse. From now on we are going to solve our problems in a spirit of reconciliation, non-partisanship, and a spirit of what is best for the most incredible country on the face of the earth.
But in the meantime this legislation is not helpful. It does not add to the debate we are going through at this very time. It does not add to the sense of security that Canadians are so desperately seeking.
Telesat Canada, via its provision of satellite services, actively supports what should be the cultural policy in Canada. It gives the appropriate underpinnings for dissemination of that cultural policy across the country. That may be taken away and left in the hands of people who may well be good people and good Canadians, but their responsibilities are to their shareholders, their boards of directors, and to a limited number of people.
The Government of Canada's responsibility is to the 25 million Canadians who care passionately not just about their future but about their ability to flourish as a country. Is it any wonder that those of us on this side of the House question this legislation? Is it any wonder that we have fears about this legislation? Is it any wonder that we say that this legislation is premature?
There may come a time when Telesat Canada should indeed go to the private sector, but it seems to me that getting rid of one of the major areas by which the government can enforce its communication policy in the midst of what is a crisis of national unity is downright stupid.
I would go further than that, except I do not want to impugn the motives of the government. I do not. I believe that the members of the government have as much of a passionate commitment to the future of Canada as do the members of the Official Opposition. I see something being done that is downright impractical

and counterproductive for a large sector of the Canadian population, for the largest segments of the country.
I see something that is going to go against the forces that we are trying to generate to keep us together. I have to speak out and say this is what we think. Please look again. Can you really believe that this is what you want to do?
There is a saying about cutting off your nose to spite your face, and I am afraid this is what this government is doing. The face of government is already unpleasant enough to the people of Canada without marring it yet one more time.

subtopic: TELESAT CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to follow my hon. colleague from Halifax on this subject. I see that she is leaving to attend a committee meeting that she has delayed me from being at myself. I was hoping she could stay and we might engage in some interesting debate after I am finished. With that disappointment I will proceed.
I am very pleased to give my support to the government's decision to sell its shares in Telesat Canada. I do so because I believe it is pertinent to our goal of enhancing the competitiveness of Canadian firms.
Enhancing Canadian competitiveness is part of our economic plan to ensure greater prosperity for all of Canada. In order to succeed we must draw on the talents and efforts of all Canadians. In today's increasingly competitive economic environment anything less will result in declining standards of living for all Canadians.
In the 1960s there was a popular song that proclaimed that times were changing. In fact times are always changing. Those who fail to adapt are doomed to be left behind. In today's environment the ability to adapt to change is fundamental to the ability to compete, as any successful business person will be able to tell you.
Allow me to explain the connection between competitiveness and government divestiture of Crown corporations and other Crown holdings such as Telesat Canada. I will be the first to admit that when government ownership of an enterprise serves a valid public policy purpose government ownership should be maintained and we should support it. The protection of Canadian technology, the nurturing of infant industries and the process of nation building are three such purposes requiring public ownership that come to mind.
However a critical examination of our Crown holdings and investments reveals a number of entities whose original raison d'etre-economic, social and cultural-have either been realized or become obsolete or, given the passage of time and events, will probably never be realized.
At one time in our history government ownership was a viable means to provide services which the private sector was unable or unwilling to provide. I would like to read some remarks that the president and chief executive officer of Telesat Canada provided to our Standing Committee on Communications and Culture recently. He recalled the beginning, in 1969, when the government enunciated its objectives in setting up its ownership of that corporation.
One objective was to provide the ability to have national radio and television networks. The satellite now does that. Before that time the CBC was available in parts of Canada and not in others. Today it is available in every town and village in the country, including the far north.
The second objective was to provide all-weather reliable communications between points in northern
November 20, 1991

Canada and between northern and southern Canada. The satellite did that and still does it. That is no longer an issue. It is here to stay.
The third objective was to provide reinforcement to heavy route east-west communications in southern Canada, and as he points out Telesat does that. One of the things it does, and few people apparently know it, is provide a back-up facility for the fibre cable networks which run east and west. When the networks are dug up by the backhoes for repair or replacement, all of the telephone traffic between Ontario and British Columbia and between British Columbia and Alberta flow over the satellite.
Eldon Thompson, chief executive officer of Telesat Canada, is by the way a New Brunswicker. In a moment I am going to read into the record the very significant performance record in recent years of that company. Eldon Thompson was a former president of N.B. Tel and has distinguished himself both in his own province and on the national scene. He says that in addition to those three original purposes for the government's involvement in Telesat Canada there was a final one. It was to give impetus to Canadian scientific development in manufacturing, and they have certainly done that. There is an export business in Canada today centred on space and satellite equipment, and in fact Telesat Canada itself exports. He points out that they currently get 6 per cent of their revenues from engineering consulting services which they deliver around the world by Canadians based in Canada.
The original purposes for government investment in Telesat Canada have been realized. I think that having justified those purposes the next threshold of achievement by Telesat Canada will be best realized in the private sector.
At one time in our history government ownership was a viable means of providing services which the private sector was unable or unwilling to provide. For the most part that time is past. Due to the maturity, diversity and dynamism of our economic infrastructure, the private sector in Canada is now able to provide the services Canadians need in most circumstances without the government's direct participation. As a private enter-
Govemment Orders
prise businessman I applaud that reality in this country. I believe it adds to the dimensions of potential which Canada faces in a very magnificent future, if we can get our current problems resolved.
Therefore in many instances the government's fiscal and human resources are being needlessly tied up in jurisdictions where they are no longer required. This is not just inefficient. It is another word for really being uncompetitive. It translates into lost market opportunities and ultimately into reduced employment.
Let me also remind my fellow members of a basic reality. More than ever before Parliament now has the available legislative powers to influence the direction of the economy strongly and resolve social problems without resorting to public ownership of corporations or joint ventures such as Telesat.
It does not take a genius to comprehend that when government ownership of private enterprise is both uncompetitive and inefficient it should be discontinued. We understood this years ago, and that is why we implemented the privatization program. While Telesat is not a Crown corporation, the sale of the government's shares in Telesat will achieve the same results and the same benefits as though it were privatization.
For example, through privatization we assist in creating new investment opportunities, new job opportunities and new market potential for Canadian firms. That is both pragmatic and rational. It is also the path which almost all of our trading partners throughout the world are following. Failing to do so ourselves will lessen our ability to compete in a world that grows more competitive every day.
We can also promote competitiveness and economic growth by liberating Crown holdings whose potential for expansion is seriously impeded by continued government ownership. By its very nature the government decisionmaking process is slow. This can seriously affect the performance of Crown holdings whose major arena of operation is the fast moving private sector, which often requires companies to react quickly to changing conditions.
Without the restraint and constraint of government ownership and its complex accountability mechanisms, these firms can generate new vigour, set new goals and create new markets.
It is perhaps appropriate at this time to read briefly from the financial statements of Telesat Canada for

November 20,1991
Government Orders
1990, just to put in perspective the significant performance of this company under government ownership. Then we may contemplate the even grander dimensions that it could achieve under the new vigour and energy that the private sector scenario provides.
In 1990 Telesat weathered a rate rollback and aggressive competition within the telecommunications marketplace. It was limited by an economic recession and still managed to increase operating revenues by an unparalleled 21 per cent over 1989. Despite operating expense increases of 11 per cent over the previous year, Telesat recorded net earnings applicable to common shares of $26.4 million, an increase of 29 per cent over 1989.
I will go on to examine the past five years of remarkable growth. In 1990 Telesat completed its first five-year period as a direct telecommunications service provider, with compound year over year revenue growth exceeding 12 per cent. Today Telesat has depth and strength on three vital fronts: as the carrier of choice to Canada's broadcasting industry, carrying signals for virtually all of Canada's national and regional broadcasters; as an important source of transmission services to other carriers and resellers; and as a direct provider of business communication network to government and industry.
In all three areas Telesat has experienced remarkable growth, characterized by the increase in its customer base over the past five years from less than 90 direct customers to more than 350 now, by an increase in its asset base from less than $600 million at the end of 1985 to $1.2 billion at the end of 1990, and by a compound year over year increase in net earnings of 20 per cent since 1985. Those are remarkable financial and economic business achievements.
One of its long-term goals is to become a world player in the next generation of satellite based personal communication systems and its 50 per cent ownership in Telesat Mobile Inc. already gives it a large stake in the North American mobile communications market. At year end it was pleased to announce the contract signing to procure Canadian and U.S. M-SAT satellites that will be operated by TMI.
That just gives a perspective of the excellence of this company, achieved with 53 per cent direct and indirect government ownership. It speaks to the threshold of
opportunity, which I am confident redirection into the private sector will bring.
In another perspective let me remind my hon. colleagues of the pressing need to bring Canada's national finances under firm control, one of the purposes of our privatization program. By reducing federal expenditures on Crown corporations or holdings such as Telesat, we will assist in reducing the federal deficit and the national debt. The rewards of doing so are an easing of inflationary pressures, the lowering of interest rates, the prospects for a strong economic recovery, sustained future growth that brings new jobs, and higher levels of prosperity.
As I have described Telesat is ripe for private ownership. We have looked at its inventory of six operating satellites and its five-year record of assisting the private sector in developing a domestic satellite communication system. The original purpose of government ownership has been achieved and it is no longer relevant. The time has come to reap the dramatic potential of this divestiture for the government, not only to assist in our expense control efforts and the contribution to our national debt reduction program but to give Telesat itself the vibrant opportunity which private ownership indeed will bring.
Telesat now provides commercial satellite systems and services nation-wide, including northern and remote areas of Canada. As my hon. colleague, the minister responsible for privatization said a few moments ago- and it was confirmed through a letter from Mr. Thompson, the chief executive officer-those services are secure and unviable. There is no prospect that the integrity of the Telesat service to northern Canada will be diminished.
For economic reasons as I explained earlier, we believe the delivery of these services is best left to the private sector. As it is, Telesat provides its services in competition with private sector telecommunications companies. While Telesat's satellite based telecommunications technology continues to benefit Canadians, securing this objective no longer requires government participation in the company. Frankly if Telesat is not exposed to the disciplines and opportunities of the private sector, then those private telecommunications companies with which it now competes will have a decided advantage. That
November 20, 1991

certainly is not in the interest of Canadians or the government. We believe that Telesat's market position will be better maintained through full private sector ownership.
The company will continue to produce and provide its services for Canadians on a commercial basis without the government sitting on its board. Telesat will thrive through a stronger incentive to succeed and the enhanced flexibility to pursue commercial opportunities. Its ability to compete will be enhanced as it becomes more innovative, more cost effective and more efficient.
Given the pressing need to enhance our national competitiveness and the state of our national finances, selling the government's Telesat Canada shares is a prudent, sensible and fiscally responsible action. Although Telesat Canada is not a Crown corporation, the sale of the government's equity interest in the company will contribute significantly toward the reduction of the federal deficit.
In closing, we on this side of the House prefer that Canadians have every opportunity to excel against our foreign competition. That is why we intend to sell our shares in this remarkable company, Telesat Canada, and thereby create new investment and market potential for the company, and new employment and investment opportunities for all Canadians.
Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley
Valley): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-38 that is being debated in the House today.
I would first like to congratulate and thank our member, the critic from Okanagan-Shuswap, who represents primarily the Vernon and Salmon Arm areas, for all of the work that he has done in this particular field. Actually, I had a chance to read Hansard and some of the comments made by the Minister of Privatization and by our member when the bill was debated on Tuesday at second reading.
I would just like to say a few things about Telesat Canada and telecommunications policy, or the lack thereof in Canada. I would also like to offer my view with respect to the current government's position as it relates to privatization and selling off public property.
Government Orders
My first comment is in regard to the privatization of Telesat Canada. As the minister outlined in his opening comments, it is technically a disposal of shares, although it is being treated very much like a privatization measure, as if it was a Crown corporation.
We have some concerns on this side of the House in terms of the government decision to dispose of Telesat Canada. Two main concerns come to mind.
Our first concern is that it is Canada's only domestic satellite system and should remain in the hands of Canadians. I was reminded of just how important telecommunications and other communications methods in the country were during the gulf war, while meeting with representatives of Canada Post. They fear that this government might just have Canada Post on the privatization block as well. The member for Mississauga cheers that notion.
This particular postmaster commented that the Government of Canada, at that point during the war, was really turning over our ability as a nation to control and regulate communications policy in the country. So there is a real concern there in terms of loosening the public control over these corporations. I will make a point later about that. I think even the minister might agree with me on some of the concerns over regulating companies in these very vital areas of communications and transportation.
The second concern, from the notes that have been provided to me, is that there is still a struggle in Canada to achieve a communications policy between the federal government and the provinces. In particular, some provinces such as Quebec have demanded to control communications policy outright. I recall previous attempts by some ministers in the government of British Columbia to control communications policy. It is my view that Telesat Canada is one of those operations that I think the Government of Canada should still have a firm hand in.
Regulation, and I think the minister might even agree with me, has become a traditional tool of government, regardless of what side of the House, to regulate and attempt to ensure that there is a minimum level of service.
I am concerned about that, and I will use transportation as an example. Deregulation has caused reduced service in the north. Yet regulation tends either to

November 20, 1991
Government Orders
guarantee monopoly or guarantee profit and actually eliminate a great deal of competition.
I will be very frank. I sometimes question the ability of regulators actually to guarantee service, be it in communications policy or transportation to the public. However at the same time there is a question about how to ensure that there is the so-called competition to guarantee that service.
I will return to the transportation example. In my community of Prince George there are two airlines competing. While there is not a great deal of difference our regulations, in this case administered by the National Transportation Agency, basically ensure that the level of service they end up providing becomes a minimum as opposed to the maximum that might be achieved. Regulations tend to create a glass ceiling. I am not sure I have a solution for that today, but it is certainly something that we have to consider and examine.
In particular, with respect to northern communities, I am especially concerned about what may be a reduction in the control that government and regulatory agencies have over various organizations like Telesat. One comment that struck me was made by a representative of one of the companies in Toronto after a journey through northern B.C. He said that he was astounded by all the satellite dishes that were around. This was a very senior representative of a communications firm who clearly had not got out of Toronto enough to realize that satellite dishes in people's backyards in northern B.C. is a very common thing.
This person was very senior in his company and obviously participated a great deal in regulatory hearings about communications policy but had no idea whatsoever about what ordinary people in a northern and remote part of British Columbia actually do. Yet agencies rely on his input into the regulatory process to develop policy. If that is what we are doing we are not going to have the best kind of policy in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the hon. member's comments about the satellite dishes in the northern parts of our country.
He may be interested to know that north of my riding, which is just north of Toronto, in the rural parts of Ontario where there is no cable service, you see a great amount of this as well. It is not just in northern Canada, but it is also in areas where there is just not the cable service, where the companies have not got in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking on this legislation.
I want to start by thanking my colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River for outlining our party's position on this legislation.
Before I proceed there seem to be philosophical ideas and proposals floating around the House today and I would like to say, for the benefit of listeners and Canadians, that I think it is important for them to also know where the Liberal Party stands on these philosophical questions.
The federal government or the Conservative philosophy calls for the private sector to do all of the work on its own. The NDP philosophy calls for the government to do everything. The Liberal Party calls for a partnership between the private sector and the public sector in order

November 20,1991
Government Orders
to achieve the best answers to our socioeconomic problems.
A member on the government side mentioned that one of the reasons this corporation is going to be sold is because we desperately need the money to put toward the deficit reduction fund.
I would like to suggest that this so-called gimmick reduction fund does not kick in until possibly 1996. As a result of that, there is really no point in trying to give the public the impression that the sale of Telesat or any corporation the federal government has interest and would in fact be used to reduce the deficit. It would be going in one way or another to the general revenues where the government could use part of that money for accounts payable.
As well my party's approach to the question of dealing with the deficit is through economic renewal, through improved productivity in the work force, through the encouragement and increase in the highly skilled work force in our society and ensuring that it is highly skilled and prepared to produce.
On the question of how to reduce the deficit, my colleague could only look at the shortfall in our society as a result of illiteracy, for instance. There is approximately $4 billion on an annual basis in lost productivity. There is $10 billion lost on an annual basis to society as a whole as a result of illiteracy. That is one area the government could focus on if it is really interested in reducing the deficit and dealing with the question of productivity in our society.
When this question came about, I could not help but read one paragraph from a release by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, recently released.
The release indicates that Canada's biggest problem is that there is a growing sense of urgency about our future economic base. Dr. Arthur May, past president of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, says that we are not keeping up with our global competitors in generating new scientific understanding in putting these gains to technological advantage.
In the report which is entitled "Ten Years to the Year 2000" a strategy makes the case that more research and
development investment and more researchers are needed to keep pace with international competition and the complex environmental problems that will face the country in the next decade.
The report, which I have here in my hand, is quite an alarming one since the subject matter deals with science and technology, telecommunications and deals with the company that is an outstanding company not only here in Canada but also all over the world. The report indicates that when it comes to the Canadian deficit in terms of buying equipment or selling equipment in science and technology, the cumulative sum is $53 billion between the period of 1978 to 1987. If you look for instance at 1987 alone our deficit in the area of science and technology comes to about $7 billion.
The report goes on to talk about Canada's research environment and talks about international comparisons which show that Canada's spending on research and development is one of the lowest of major industrialized nations. In fact, according to the 1987 statistics, it shows Canada at a 1.38 per cent standing when it comes to those expenditures on research and development as a result of the Gross Domestic Product. That is far below countries such as the United States at 2.83 per cent and Japan at 2.78 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, when you look at 1986 the total expenditure in Canada was approximately $5.6 billion, which was a minimal amount when you compare it to the United States of $117.4 billion, or when you look at Japan spending $41.8 billion in the area of science research and development.
When we look at the research and development expenditures over the last 15 years, what we have been seeing in Canada is a decline in terms of expenditures.
Canada's poor research and development performance is a cause for alarm. There is no question about it. If we are really serious about increasing our society's investment in research and development, we cannot forget the fact that the federal government has a role in the field and that is leadership.
That is why I wanted to just give this very brief introduction about the state of our society when it comes to research and development and where we compare with the rest of the world to clearly state the case for not selling our shares in Telesat Canada. The reason why we
November 20, 1991

should not be selling our shares in Telesat Canada is that Telesat Canada has proven not only to the rest of the industries in Canada but to industries around the world that it is a leading force among other industries in the area of telecommunications such at Northern Telecom and many others.
Mr. Speaker, if you will recall, when Telesat Canada was established under the Telesat Canada Act in 1969, it was a joint venture between the Government of Canada of the day and the major Canadian telecommunications industry. The purpose of it at the time was to develop a domestic satellite based telecommunications systems and services. As of today, Telesat is the only Canadian company that provides commercial satellite facilities and services across Canada. It is also the only Canadian company that provides basic telecommunications facilities to northern communities and to remote regions in Canada.
Telesat owns and operates six satellites and a network of approximately 500 earth stations. It has launched two satellites this year, Anik-1 and Anik-2. The company's revenues are derived from leasing satellite capacity to major television broadcasting companies, to Telecom Canada members and to other smaller firms that provide specialized value added telecommunications services.
Telesat also earns revenues through the provision of voice, data and imaging services to businesses in direct competition with Unitel, telephone companies and enhanced telecommunications service providers. The company also offers international telecommunication consulting services.
The reason why I define all those points is to give you a profile of Telesat and the kind of services it provides to the Canadian public. But of more interest, it is important to outline that in terms of revenue. In 1989 the net earnings were approximately $23 million; in 1990 the net earnings were $30.5 million. This is not a white elephant; this is a profitable company, this is a leading company in the area of telecommunications. It is profitable.
One would suggest that rather than just selling our shares in Telesat, we should be using those shares as a leverage, as a means for our government and for our society to play a leading role as an example for the rest of the industries in the area of science and technology so
Government Orders
that they can invest more in research and development and not less.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the situation here in Canada is that individual industries, individual companies are spending less on research and development. The government knows that, the industry knows that, the experts know that, and everybody is talking about the need for more investment in research and development. Since we have this leverage, I would suggest we should be using it and not abandoning it.
I cannot help but go back to the report which was released by the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council of Canada. On page 10 the writers talk about political initiatives. This is a very important point, Mr. Speaker. They talk about the fact that we as a society must develop a cohesive science and technology policy and invest more in research and development. They make the statement acknowledging the fact that by the year 2000 over 60 per cent of all jobs in our society are going to require at least 16 years of education. More and more we are becoming a society that depends on an information based industry, that we are becoming a society that needs a highly skilled work force.
I do not think that by letting our shares be put on the selling block that we are setting a good example, in fact, we should be doing the opposite. We should be investing more. Someone was asking me why. Why invest more? Because in all of the leading countries around the world in the area of space research there is government involvement. I would bet you, Mr. Speaker, that if it were not for the American government intervention in the area of space technology, they would not have been able to put a man on the moon.
This is no different for other countries such as the Soviet Union. If it had not been for the intervention of the government in the Soviet Union it would not have been able to achieve what it has achieved in the area. It is the same for Japan, France and all the countries around the world on the leading edge in this area.
I wonder about the wisdom of selling our interest in one of the finest companies in the world, Telesat. On an annual basis the revenues of the industry, especially in the telecommunications area, are in excess of $21 billion on an annual basis. If there is any flag that we as

November 20, 1991
Government Orders
Canadians could cany with a lot of pride it is the flag of the telecommunications industry. At this point I am at a loss to see ourselves moving ahead with this sale.

The government does not own them.
That is where I part company with the hon. member. I cannot understand why a government has to be in business in order to participate, promote or encourage research and development and entrepreneurship. I agree with the hon. member when he said earlier: "There is a time and a place for Crown corporations". The Progressive Conservatives established many of the Crown corporations we have today. There is no question about that.
In my opening remarks I said that there is a time and a place when governments should become involved, that is if the private sector is not prepared to do what has to be done or does not have the expertise. A country matures. An industry matures. As that progression takes place governments have the mandate to change. We cannot stay the way we were. Our parents and grandparents would love us to stay exactly the way we were. However things are moving too fast for that.
I part company with my friend who said: "In order for us to participate and promote and encourage we have to own". That sounds an awful lot like NDP philosophy. He said that the Conservatives think that the private sector can do everything. Obviously it cannot or we would have privatized everything, which we have not done. We have privatized those companies that no longer serve a public policy purpose. I am surprised, because he is a clear thinking individual, that he would support the philosophy that you must own in order to promote, regulate or participate.

Mr. Speaker, to differentiate us from the NDP we are not calling on the government to do everything. In fact we are calling on the government to be in a partnership with the private sector. Mr. Speaker, if you review the "blues" you will find that was the thrust of my presentation today.
The reasons that the government got involved in the area of research and development in 1969, the motives at that time, should be the same motives followed by the government today in the area of research and development. There has not really been any tremendous improvement in private sector investment in research and development since 1975 when contrasted with what the government has been investing in the area of research and development. Even with its involvement in research and development the government has not been able to kick start private sector investment.
It is not good enough for us to say that it did not work in the past and it did not work after 1969 when we set up the act and all those Crown corporations, so we can abandon it now. We have to be even more persistent because of the failure of the private sector to invest more in the area of research and development. We must lead the way, in partnership with the private sector. By no means am I saying that we should be taking over the industry and running it. Socialist or communist movements around the world have shown us that government-run operations do not necessarily prove to be that successful all the time. There is something to say about the need for one major industry in our society that is big, capable, and produces a solid product.
Simply put, Telesat Canada is that particular corporation. It has a world-wide reputation. We can use it as as an example for the rest of the industry. We could say that this is a situation where the government owned a little under 50 per cent and the private sector owned a little over 50 per cent. It could be a model for partnership between the private sector and public sectors. We could say: "Here is our money" and ask the private sector to put its money out all across the board. The end result would be a healthier industry that could be beneficial for our society and also could help us enter the 21st century as a leading force, especially in the area of research and

I cannot help but mention to my colleagues that when comparing the number of scientists and engineers in Canada with Japan you would find that in Japan there are approximately 10 times more engineers than in Canada but in Canada there are 20 times more lawyers than in Japan. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on this bill, at this stage in opposition to it.
This country did not naturally evolve as a result of geographic or economic forces but was a creation of public policy.
A very small group of Canadians in a small section of the eastern part of this great continent decided that over a period of time they could actually create a nation extending from coast to coast. There were two essential elements to achieving that public policy objective. One was a good transportation system and the other was, increasingly important as time went on, a good communications system.
Those two were achieved by a number of instruments of public policy. One of those was ownership of the means of communication and the means of transportation which were not economically viable in such a geographically large country with such a small and scattered population.
Those instruments became more sophisticated as time went on. Telesat certainly has been one of those instruments of public policy to bring Canada's communications system into, not only the next century, but the next millennium.
The minister said that companies mature. I suppose this is one of those companies that has reached a certain stage of maturity. However the issue really is whether it and the nation have reached the stage of maturity where

November 20,1991
Government Orders
there is no longer a public interest in majority ownership of Telesat Canada.
As companies mature, so too do countries. This country is far from maturity. We are still a very small population scattered across a small fraction of our territory. The idea of nationhood still hangs together on very slim fibres of transportation and communications connections. Essentially it is Telesat Canada which has guaranteed that modern advances in communications technology will benefit not only the populated areas of southern Canada, the large fraction of our population of Canadians that live in major urban centres, but all those who live in remote areas, those who live in our northern regions, those who belong to Canada in a real sense only by the communication and transportation connections they have with the rest of Canada.
As companies and countries mature, the issue before us is, has this country matured to the point where there is no longer a public policy purpose for a company like Telesat Canada. I do not believe so and my party does not believe so.
Satellite communication is, in many senses, still in its infancy. The potentials that were set out in the original mandate of Telesat Canada are far from being achieved. The potential of Canada as a leading nation in the field of telecommunications are in their infancy and far from being achieved.
What I see in this bill is the intent to sell off and privatize a big chunk of our future because the future of this country right now is mostly potential. What we have to accomplish is still ahead of us and eroding the foundation on which that future will be built is not in the interests of this generation or of generations to come.
The minister mentioned that management is anxious to get on with privatization. Frankly that is not an argument that carries much weight with me. Over a number of privatizations, I have seen management anxious to get on with privatization often because it is to their benefit to do so. One of the statements on the public airwaves that has made me angriest in the last couple of years was, at the time, chief executive officer, president, whatever, of Air Canada on Cross Canada Check-up saying: "Privatize Air Canada and give me the freedom and I will run this company the way it should be run".
I nearly dove through the radio because I said to myself: "If you can run the company better than you are running it now, then why are you not doing it for the people of Canada who have invested in this company." I say the same thing to management of Telesat Canada: "If you can run it better, run it better". It should not make any difference whether you are doing it for your fellow Canadians as majority owners or for private companies as majority owners.
The straight and honest reason why this argument does not carry much weight with me is because there has seldom been a privatization from which management has not benefited financially and personally. They are seldom in a situation where the privatization has not been set up in a way to make sure that happens. So that is not a veiy convincing argument from the minister from my point of view.
The government obviously feels it is important to maintain the monopoly position of Telesat Canada and yet to remove it from regulation at the same time. That is a very delicate balance to start disturbing. Why I say the government feels that the monopoly should be maintained is that the bill does not provide for, but the government has stated, its intention to maintain that monopoly position for 10 years. However, it does not deal with what happens at the end of 10 years. What is the mechanism for maintaining the monopoly? If there is a benefit to the government continuing to intervene even after it has privatized the company, what is the balance between its continued intervention on behalf of the company in the marketplace and the benefits of continued public ownership.
It seems to me that this bill comes forward, as the numbers seem to do, in the area of privatization and in the area of telecommunications and in the area of transportation, without a very solid policy foundation, without a serious understanding of where we are heading in the future in a number of these domains.
Let me just give you a couple of examples of what I mean by that. Telecommunications and Telesat as part of that industry in Canada has a significant role to play not only in communications within Canada but in Canada's position in the international communications market.
November 20, 1991

Yet we have a vacuum of policy on communications. Where are we heading on communications? What is the intention of this government? I simply do not think it is good enough to bring forward piecemeal legislation without it being in the context of a policy direction that is demonstrably to the benefit of Canada and Canadians.
Second, we have a vacuum of policy in the area of global trade. We have no clear direction of what kind of market niches this country intends to carve out for itself in the future. We have, it seems to me, no policy that is based on at least an understanding and interpretation of where we think the world is heading, where we think the opportunities are and how we are going to mesh our expertise in various fields, how we are going to start developing new possibilities, new technology, how we are going to frame our education and our training programs in this country to allow Canadians to fit into that world of the future.
I hear a lot of words like global trade and competitiveness but I see no policy foundation on which we are making unique and discrete decisions that will help us as a nation be part of the world of tomorrow.
I see a vacuum of policy on research and development. We are seeing again the further erosion of basic research at the National Research Council. I have spoken on that in this House more than once, but again, no policy on research and development in Canada. There is no sense of future direction that is related to the global marketplace and what Canada will need to be strong in the future in that global marketplace.
Instead, we have traded off long-term prospects for short-term prospects. As we continue to clip the flowers off the research and development tree, which is the direction I see this government heading, we are forgetting to water the roots.
The minister mentioned that government does not have to be owner of a company or owner in an industry to participate in research and development in that industry and that is perfectly true. On the other hand, I see no policy direction with respect to this bill that says: What is the role of government in research and development in the telecommunications field?
We know as well that the use of satellite telecommunications is now and will be increasingly important in the
Government Orders
whole area of solving environmental problems, understanding them and applying the technology to deal with some of those environmental problems.
A public policy role for telecommunications in dealing with our environmental degradation world-wide is extremely important. Yet there is no sense, no policy for Canada to be following on how we should be investing in research and development in the environmental area. There is no discussion even of how abandoning the public role in the provision of satellite services in Canada will affect the potential that Canada might have to be an active world leader in some of those environmental applications of satellite and other telecommunications technology.
The minister says that there will be a 10-year monopoly but we do not really know that. In 10 years, what has happened? Is it quite all right with us that satellite accessibility to Canada, to Canadian carriers is only available through companies outside Canada, through satellites that are unconnected to Canada as a nation?
The government has an obligation to answer all these questions and to deal with these issues before it starts selling off piece by piece, part of the infrastructure that allows us to explore as a nation our full economic potential in the world, our full potential to contribute and to benefit internationally from telecommunications, our policy on research and development in many of the areas that the involving world is going to need and our role in environmental research and applications which are at least in one sector strongly linked to communications ability.
I want to mention the situation of one individual because I think it is relevant to this. A scientist who used to work in Canada and then with the sell-off of a major airline company was forced to move to the United States to find work. After two years he was back here this summer putting a serious effort into finding work in Canada. This is a man who has had international training, who is highly specialized in fields that are of significance to Canada in our future scientific research and technology endeavours. There is no place for him in Canada. There is no place for him in government, in the private sector and meanwhile Canadian companies and government departments are importing similar talents from other parts of the world.

November 20, 1991
Government Orders
If we do not settle where we are going in research and development, it will soon be too late to encourage young Canadians to go into the specialized fields that this country needs. It will be too late to keep them here. It will be too late to have companies with a culture of developing, promoting and using Canadian talent.
This is just one of many stories. This country has lost one brilliant scientist who should be, who wants to be, working here in Canada for the future of Canada.
This whole communications area is one in which Canada has been very much on the leading edge. We have been on the leading edge because of public involvement in the telecommunications industry.
In bringing forward the bill, as it has done today, in a vacuum of policy in a number of areas, the government is saying: "We are getting out of that", and it is giving us no assurances whatsoever that it even considers it important for Canada to stay at that leading edge. I consider that somewhat of an abandonment of responsibility to the future.
I want to take the one or two minutes left to me to speak about the hocus-pocus of deficit reduction. It is a great game that is being played these days of dividing the money up in four different pockets, three different pockets, ten different pockets and saying: "We are using this pocket to pay for this and this pocket to pay for that and somehow we will create a separate little pocket for deficit reduction and it will mean we are spending more on deficit reduction". Nonsense. The money comes in in one lump sum and it does not matter how many pockets you divide it into, it is how you are spending it that determines what your deficit is or is not going to be.
It is also true that one way to reduce the deficit is to get rid of the debt we are carrying. If the government is serious about using revenues to reduce the burden on taxpayers then the way to do that is to lower the debt we are carrying. That is not happening. What is happening is that debt is constantly increasing, but every householder out there knows that until you pay off your mortgage you are continually paying for your mortgage. We cannot have every major error in public policy justified by somehow it is going to reduce the deficit. Spending patterns are what creates or will reduce the deficit.
Nothing else. The government knows that and Canadians are not buying the line.
There are a number of policy areas that seriously need to be addressed by this government if the future for Canada is going to hold the same promise and potential that the past has held. I do not think that taking a step like this in a vacuum of policy direction is a wise thing to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment about the minister's comment. I find it fascinating that I said virtually nothing my colleague before did not say and the policy perspectives which the minister chose to compliment him on. Frankly, I find it a little bit condescending for the minister to refer to my "little speech" and the fact that I probably have not read a report, neither of which is true.
I think it is fascinating that the minister chose to make two totally different sets of comments on two speeches with virtually the same content.
I want to respond particularly to his points because the minister has precisely made my point. In fact, the paper he referred to, as I understand it, is a discussion paper. It is out there for discussion and makes precisely the point that those policy directions are not in place. The minister said: "Well, yes, there has been a lot of change in the world". Precisely when there is a lot of change happening one needs to have a clear sense of what are the strengths of this country, what is our future direction and where do we want to fit so we can adapt to those changes. That is not in fact what I see from the government and it is certainly not what I see in terms of our communications policy on an international level or environmental policy on an international level or our research and development policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate it if the Speaker, who is a good friend of mine, would take the trouble to memorize the name of my riding.
As you know, I am very proud to represent the riding of Carleton-Gloucester. As for today's debate on Bill C-38 which provides for the sale of Telesat Canada by the government, I am also proud to say that the company is located in the municipality where I have been a resident for quite some time, and I am referring to the municipality or city of Gloucester.
Government Orders
Some years ago I had the privilege of being a member of Gloucester City Council which was actively involved in bringing Telesat Canada to Gloucester. We were very lucky, because despite some very stiff competition from a number of municipalities in the region which all wanted to have Telesat Canada within their borders, the company fortunately located in the city of Gloucester.
Telesat has 877 employees, 672 of whom are based in Gloucester, at the head office.

Telesat Canada is a profitable satellite communications company which is based, as I said, in Gloucester, my home town. Telesat is jointly owned by the federal government at 53 per cent or over 51 per cent and Canada's largest telephone companies. It is the only commercial communications satellite operator in Canada and derives most of its revenues from leasing satellite channels to broadcasters and telephone companies.
Telesat is regulated by the CRTC. The Telesat Canada Act was passed in 1969. The objects of the Telesat Act are set out in Telesat as follows: (a) establish satellite telecommunication systems providing, on a commercial basis, telecommunication services between locations in Canada and subject to the appropriate intergovernmental arrangements; (b) supply on a commercial basis satellite telecommunication systems and elements thereof in Canada or elsewhere; and (c) provide on a commercial basis services associated with the development, implementation and operation of satellite telecommunication systems and elements thereof in Canada or elsewhere.
The old legislation also contained safeguards which, not incorporated in Bill C-38, provided for the use of Canadian research design and industrial personnel, technology and facilities in research and development connected with satellite telecommunication systems and the design and the construction of the systems. It was truly a Canadian company dedicated to pursuing technological advances in the satellite telecommunication industry.
The government is promising that Telesat will maintain its monopoly on the provision of satellite telecommunication services for the next 10 years. However, it is not including that provision in the legislation. What happens after 10 years? What happens after this lease on public policy expires?

November 20, 1991
Government Orders
With regard to the global competition, while the government may have achieved part of the public purpose objective domestically, it has not fully achieved any extra-domestic or global objective which was permitted in the original legislation creating Telesat. The global competition challenge continues today more than ever and that should not be removed from Telesat's mandate, as is being done by and with the new legislation. The words authorizing non-domestic commercial initiatives in Telesat's objects are removed in this new bill.
The government may be taking Canada out of a high tech communications sector with a future in the global economy rather than making Telesat and Canada a leader and innovator in the field. Telesat has had the leading edge on the provisions of satellite telecommunications services. Rather than expanding and building on that edge, the government is saying that we have fulfilled the public policy purpose and is getting out.
The Americans would not have put the first man on the moon without the involvement of the American government. The private sector did not do it in the U.S. or in the U.S.S.R. when it put the first man in space. The government is so convinced by the ideology of its friends in the private sector it is now going to turn over this whole enterprise to it.
The government claims that it is disposing of the shares of its holdings in Telesat in its continuing efforts to reduce the deficit, and yet only the net proceeds of the sale of government shares will go to the deficit reduction fund. Why not the gross amount? The government appears to want to keep the $30 million book value for its own purpose. What is that purpose?
In research and development, Bill C-38 makes no provision for the continued use of Canadian research, design and industrial personnel, technology and facilities in research and development connected with satellite telecommunication systems, and the design and construction of the systems. The government is promising that a condition of sale will be a requirement that Telesat continue to give Canadian suppliers of satellites and major earth station equipment first consideration in their purchase decisions. However, there are no guarantees that such practices will be observed once the
government's shares of Telesat are sold. How will the government require that first consideration is given to Canadian suppliers? Does this breach GATT national treatment requirements? Is that why it is not in the bill?
I feel this is a back door deregulation. Section 14 of Bill C-38 provides a glimpse at the possibility of back door deregulation in Canadian telecommunications when it states that the CRTC may refrain from regulating Telesat activities under certain conditions. In legal jargon, the term used is "forbearance". Should it be the CRTC or Parliament which decides whether deregulation should occur?
Current Telesat shareholder Bell Canada is saying that it may dump its 25 per cent stake in Telesat if the government's 51-plus per cent shareholdings fall into unfriendly hands, such as a rival company like Canadian Pacific, for example. Bell is said to have been a potential suitor of the soon-to-be private Telesat. Will privatization destabilize and undermine both the market and the future role of Telesat if it is proceeded with through the open bidding process?
Telesat owns and operates six satellites, a network of approximately 500 earth stations, and has launched two satellites this year, the Anik-E2 and Anik-El.
The company's revenues are derived from leasing satellite capacity to major television broadcasting companies, Telecom Canada members, and numerous smaller firms that provide specialized value-added telecommunications services.
Telesat also earns revenues through the provision of voice, data and imaging services to businesses in direct competition with Unitel, the telephone companies and enhanced telecommunications service providers.
Finally the company offers international telecommunications consulting services. As I was saying, the Government of Canada owns 49.3 per cent of the shares of Telesat Canada and this coupled with what the CN owns amounts to over 51 per cent.
The financial position of Telesat Canada is as follows. In 1990 the operations revenues were $177.8 million. The net earnings were $30.4 million. The total shareholder equity is $282.4 million. The return on investment in 1987 was 10.8 per cent, and in 1990 is now 12 per cent. The book value is $34.54 per share. Telesat Canada has
November 20, 1991

doubled revenues in the past 10 years and government has a $30 million loan to Telesat Canada.
Why are we dumping Telesat Canada if it is such a good deal? The disposition issue is in my mind. The government will put toward the national debt plus the servicing the net value of the loan after sale. Then how much money is expected to go toward the debt after the sale, if we subtract the $30 million loan and the costs involved in transferring this loan.
My great concern here is the access to information after sale. We are going to have a possible sale of well over $150 million of Canadian shares. Will we have accountability of the disposition? The government has a poor track record in access to information. Take for example the case of de Havilland. Details have been kept secret because it was done, we were told, by Order in Council and therefore kept secret from the Canadian public.
I would like to know from the government minister once the sale is made-and I point out that I disagree with the sale-whether there will be full accountability of the disposition so that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, for example, can have a thorough look at money for value here. Are we doing the right thing?
In conclusion, in the Canadian way of life, government, community and business often get together as they have in the past to create des entreprises that are very successful. Why does the present government want to bash this way of life and sell off the Canadian ownership in these industries to whom I presume can only be their friends?

The objectives which my hon. friend read, for which that arrangement was made in 1969, have now been met and are no longer required.
