speechtext: The House resumed from Tbesday, October 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Blaikie that Bill C-204, an act to amend the Atomic Energy Control Act (ending development and exportation of prescribed items and substances), be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee D.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is the largest exporter of uranium in the world. Indeed, my province of Saskatchewan has over 20 per cent of world uranium production. Cameco Corporation headquartered in Saskatoon is one of the world's largest producers of uranium. It supplies uranium fuel to electrical utilities throughout the world.
Cameco alone employs 1,200 people in Canada and more than two-thirds of those in Saskatchewan. Indeed, in northern Saskatchewan Cameco is the largest single private sector employer. The Canadian uranium industry

November 20, 1991
Private Members' Business
in total accounted for more than $850 million in export sales in 1990.
Canada has developed a world class nuclear technology which satisfies the stringent standards and procedures that are required by the Atomic Energy Control Board. Candu units in Canada supply close to half of Ontario's electricity, about 30 per cent of that of New Brunswick and altogether more than 15 per cent of Canada's total electricity. In 1990 about 17 per cent of the world's electricity was generated by over 400 nuclear power plants operating in 24 countries. So nuclear power is indeed a factor in today's world and we must continue to ensure that it is managed well by qualified and experienced people to serve the needs of the public in a safe and reliable manner.
In the health field, hundreds of thousands of people are undergoing treatment involving radioisotopes, the production of which require a nuclear reactor.
Cobalt 60 is a manufactured isotope used for a variety of medical uses. The Canadian company Nordion International is the world's major supplier of Cobalt 60, which is produced under a contract in Candu nuclear power reactors. Nordion also provides most other reactor produced radioisotopes used around the world, primarily in medical diagnosis. The Canadian industry's pioneering work in nuclear medicine has been instrumental in improving the health of individuals all over the world. Indeed over 500,000 patients in more than 80 countries are treated annually using Canadian nuclear technology.
The use of radioisotopes goes beyond the medical field into other areas of health. Nuclear research has resulted in the development of new plant strains, with higher yields and greater disease resistance. Other applications in agriculture determine the soil moisture in different land areas and their abilities to meet the water needs of specific crops and to track the way crops take up nutrients as a step toward improving fertilizers.
Still another application is to trace the ground water movement of contaminated streams in order to ensure that drinking water intakes are not at risk.
As well, food irradiation promises to improve our ability to preserve food while at the same time reducing the incidence of food-borne diseases. The process for the preservation of food is an area of extraordinary potential significance to Canada and the Third World.
An enormously important additional health benefit to nuclear energy stems from the fact that no pollution from combustion products results from the process of nuclear reaction. Nuclear power emits no greenhouse gases, no sulphur dioxide, no carbon dioxide.
The use of nuclear generated electricity for energy applications that currently use fossil fuels will reduce emissions of both greenhouse gases and acid gases which cause acid rain.
It is obvious that renewable means of providing electricity such as wind, solar and tidal power will not come near to meeting Canada's growing needs. We must face the challenge of producing greater quantities of electricity in a clean fashion, thereby protecting the environment and ultimately the health of Canadians.
Passage of Bill C-204 would compromise Canada's successful nuclear power program and the continued supply of radioisotopes for medical treatment and diagnostic purposes. Bill C-204 puts in jeopardy Canada's highly regarded reputation as a reliable and stable international trading partner. No doubt Canada's competitors would take full advantage of this opportunity. The Canadian uranium industry and its mining, processing, exploration and development, which attracts additional major international investment into Canada would be put at risk.
Canada just sold one of its world class reactors to Korea. This sale will inject over $400 million into the Canadian economy. Further orders would strengthen the high-tech part of Canadian industry. There are over
100,000	Canadian jobs dependent on the nuclear history. The viability of the Candu must not be jeopardized by the threat of the moratorium proposed in Bill C-204.
The benefits of nuclear energy that I have addressed today are primarily associated with medical and health services provided by the use of radioisotopes generated in nuclear reactors. These benefits to Canadians, along with many others discussed by previous participants in this debate, clearly indicate the need to preserve and protect Canada's nuclear industry. I urge hon. members to oppose Bill C-204.
